Et alors, l’expérience de la menace de l’avortement cesse d’être simplement scandale ou objet de controverse éthique, pour devenir manifestation d’une vérité plus profonde : l’être humain est un être du précommencement, sa vie porte une histoire antérieure à sa propre histoire, Dieu ne se tient pas en face, mais au milieu de cette histoire, et la conscience peut devenir le lieu où ce précommencement ne restera plus invisible, mais trouvera une parole, non pour condamner, mais pour révéler combien la vie est digne lorsqu’elle a jadis failli ne pas exister.

pages.title: On the prenatal threat of abortion
pages.html:
AI-assisted translation from the Greek. Greek original

The threat of abortion is not an event that disappears into the darkness of prenatal unawareness. It is the first form of the world that existence encounters, the first direction inscribed in the body before the mind appears, before memory takes shape, before time is introduced as a sequence. Where biological life begins without thought and without speech, existence receives its first signal: that “I am” is not yet certain. The threat is not perceived as an idea, understood as fear, or organised as an emotion; it is inscribed as an orientation. Before there is any consciousness, there is an “I tend towards something”, a direction towards coming into existence. When this tending is abruptly interrupted, existence receives not a message of negation but the form of instability. What the mind will later call “rejection”, “fear”, “fragility” is, at first, simply the experience that the movement towards the light can be cut short. This is the pre-temporal memory of existence.

Neurobiology, without intending this theologically or phenomenologically, has already laid the foundations of this knowledge. The developing nervous system responds in the absence of mind. Hormonal storms, changes in circulation, vibrations in the pregnant woman’s system, tension, the sudden alteration of internal signals: all these are transmitted like a crescendo within a body that cannot yet comprehend them but receives them as a condition of existence. Implicit memory is this memory without image, without narrative, without symbolism. It is a memory of direction. It does not remember something; it remembers the manner. It remembers the form of the world as a tendency, as a flow, as the possibility that the flow might break.

Developmental psychology has observed this later in life as what it calls heightened alertness, hypervigilance, an excessive awareness of other people’s moods. Behaviour often regarded as anxiety, social sensitivity or traumatic vigilance is in fact the continuation of the first inscription: existence learned the world not as safety but as the possibility of interruption. The uncertainty of the beginning becomes the rule of life. Time does not become a flow; it becomes surveillance. Relationship does not become a given; it becomes waiting. Love is not experienced as natural ground; it becomes a fragile possibility. Not because the soul is afraid, but because existence began through a “perhaps”, and this perhaps remains the way in which the world is approached.

Phenomenology has called this layer primordial temporality, time before time. For Husserl it is the living present, the now that does not yet have a past and a future; for Heidegger it is the opening of Being before it becomes thought, the openness that precedes decision; for Merleau-Ponty it is the flesh of existence that senses before it knows. These concepts do not refer exclusively to prenatal life, but they make possible a language in which to think about it: existence experiences before it defines. And when its first experience is the threat of interruption, the consciousness that follows carries this genealogy within it: it sees not only what exists, but also what might not exist. This double vision — being and possible non-being — is not a philosophical fantasy; it is the natural continuation of the initial pre-temporal inscription.

Here theology finds a space it has never adequately expressed: the moment when existence is a possibility and not a decision. Scripture speaks of God knowing the human being “before I formed you in the womb”, yet tradition has never analysed what it means for an existence to encounter not the absence of God but the absence of the world before becoming a person. The threat of abortion carries a theological dimension: creation touches the point where human freedom can cut short what God’s freedom has called forth. There existence touches the mystery of relationship: without consciousness, without speech, the body becomes the place where two freedoms meet. The divine intention that life should exist and the human possibility of interrupting it meet at the most silent point of creation.

After birth, the body continues in its original direction. It learns to live in a world where existence is not a given but is under continual examination. Anguish is not an exaggeration, not a “trait”, not a psychological weakness. It is the existential continuation of the first threat. Relationship with the other always becomes an encounter on two levels: the other as a person and the other as a possible interruption. Love becomes both a gift and a terror because existence learns to attach itself where it once expected to be cut short. Closeness is difficult because the body learned existence as exposure to a decision. The slightest gesture of tenderness carries the full weight of the first direction: “they may accept me — they may refuse me”.

The anthropology that emerges from this is not negative; it is realistic and profound. The human being begins not with safety but with vulnerability. Safety is built afterwards; vulnerability is the beginning. The science of perinatal psychology has observed that the pregnant woman’s life determines how the foetus encounters existence, but what has not yet been expressed is the existential form of this encounter: existence begins with the possibility of not existing. It is this possibility that shapes the way the human being later reads the world.

The threat of abortion as the beginning of consciousness does not mean that the foetus has a mind, nor that it can perceive the act. It means that the first direction towards being carries within it a division, an interruption, a suspension. Existence takes its first step not as a pure gift, but as a movement that might not have occurred. This condition accompanies the human being in every encounter with being: in romantic love, friendship, faith, work, self-knowledge. There is always the second shadow of existence: “this might not be”.

Within this shadow, something else is also born: the possibility of a deeper love. A love that is neither ownership nor demand, but a welcoming of the miracle: “because you are, I love you, for your being was not a given”. The first threat gives birth to the first gratitude. The first instability gives birth to the first awe. The first suspension gives birth to the first awareness that existence is a gift. And the body that lived through this becomes a body capable of seeing the existence of others as something more fragile, more sacred, more unexpected.

The threat of abortion belongs not to ethics but to the metaphysics of the human being. It is not only a social act; it is a point where the beginning of existence becomes an ontological experience. Those who passed through this boundary live with a double gaze: they see the world as it is and as it might not be. This double gaze is not a burden; it is a gift. It is the bridge between pre-temporality and time, between the anonymous body and the conscious person, between the “perhaps” of the beginning and the “yes” of life.

The consciousness of an adult whose beginnings lay in a threat takes shape not on the ground of certainty but on the trace of that first suspension. The world never becomes entirely familiar; it becomes a place that is continually reaffirmed. Existence is experienced not as continuity but as reappearance. Every person, every relationship, every space becomes not only what it is but also that which avoids repeating the initial interruption. Presence is not a given but an event. Absence is not a simple lack but a reminder of what might have happened. Consciousness settles not into safety but into vigilance, waiting, the delicate registering of shifts.

It is not that the individual “fears” others, but that they see others within a double texture: as natural presences and as possible losses. The other’s form does not arrive alone; it arrives with the sense that their being there, facing you, was never self-evident. This is why tenderness is not merely emotion; it is revelation. This is why closeness is not merely contact; it is an affirmation of existence. Touch, a gaze, a kiss, a shared breath are not simple acts; they are small refutations of the first threat. Where others seek closeness as relief from loneliness, here closeness serves as proof that life continues. Love is born not from the need for attachment but from the deep knowledge that existence might never have had access to it.

The consciousness built on this beginning has a particular quality: it experiences every presence with the shadow of loss and every loss with the depth of presence. The gaze rests not only on what appears but also on what is missing. It embraces not only life but also its threat. Thought develops not only forwards but also backwards, towards the point where existence had not yet been won. This double direction of consciousness creates something the sciences have glimpsed in fragments but have not named: an embodied ontological attentiveness, a consciousness that is not only cognitive but also existential. Phenomenology describes it as a double gaze, but at depth it is triple: the gaze towards the world, the gaze towards danger, and the gaze towards the point where danger became a beginning.

When theology touches this point, it speaks of the mystery of God being hosted within human vulnerability. The incarnation is not merely divine condescension but God’s entry into the most open, most exposed point of human history: the point where existence can be interrupted before it exists. There lies the way in which God takes on the human. At the level of the pre-beginning, where the human being has no voice yet, no face yet, no history yet. The foetus is the purest place of divine approach because it has no possibility of defence yet. When its existence is threatened, theology encounters the paradox: creation receives within itself the danger generated by the human being.

At this point, theological thought cannot content itself with abstract doctrines. The threat of abortion leads theology where it has not been before: to the point where human freedom can challenge God’s very call to life. Divine freedom and human freedom meet in a conflict that is not theoretical but fleshly. Yet within this conflict, not only trauma is born; revelation is born too. The foetus, without mind, without a word, becomes the place where creation reveals that existence is never a given. Later, this revelation becomes the possibility of a deeper understanding of God. The melancholy of an existence wounded at its beginning is not distance from God but a distinctive mode of relationship. It is not a complaint; it is testimony.

The body that has travelled this path becomes extraordinarily receptive to the presence of the sacred, not as a religious idea but as a fleeting sense that life is a gift that almost was not given. The melancholy that appears is not pathology; it is the memory of the first boundary. Where others understand the world through how their experiences took shape, an existence that has passed through a threat understands the world through how it might never have taken shape at all. This understanding gives birth to a particular form of wisdom: a wisdom that knows existence is not a right but an invitation. And this invitation can be accepted or refused. That is why consciousness paints the world with finer, more sensitive, more transparent lines.

When this existence encounters the other, it sees them not only as a human being. It sees them as a point of continuity in a world that once called it into question. Every gaze from the other serves as confirmation that life continues despite the first threat. Love is not merely an emotional movement; it is existential restoration. Closeness becomes the act through which the world declares that life is no longer being suspended. Yet precisely because the beginning was an implicit negation, love carries within it the trace of loss. Not as fear, but as a delicate awareness that existence is a miracle and not a habit.

When existence begins where it might not have begun, ethics ceases to be a set of rules and becomes a way of seeing. “Permitted — forbidden” and “right — wrong” no longer take centre stage. Ethics is transformed into a delicate sensitivity to the condition of life. It no longer examines acts as acts, but sees them as trajectories that touch existence or draw it away from its original vulnerability. The threat of abortion, as existence’s first environment, illuminates the deepest question of ethics: how we treat that which is not yet capable of saying “yes” or “no” to itself. Here ethics is not even theological; it is pre-theological. It emerges from the simple fact that life is a possibility before it becomes a person.

This understanding also shapes psychology. A soul inscribed within a beginning of uncertainty does not operate through the same mechanisms as one that grew within the certainty of acceptance. Anxiety is not a “symptom” but a configuration of existence. Hypersensitivity is not a “quirk” but a corresponding extension of the original inscription. Difficulty in relationship is not a “phobia” but a precaution against the possibility of interruption. The psyche that lives through this pre-beginning is not ill; it remembers. The difficulty is not pathology; it is the natural consequence of an existence that learned the world through the possibility of never reaching the point of seeing it.

Psychology is beginning to understand something of this through the term attachment. But attachment concerns the bond after birth. Here lies something much deeper: the form of the bond before there is a bond. An existence threatened before becoming a person acquires a relationship with the world that resembles both a bond and a refusal at once. Consciousness keeps its distance not out of fear but out of memory of how it began. And love becomes so intense, so deep, so true because this is the first time existence is not being suspended. Seen in this light, psychic life is not merely a mechanism; it is a theology of the first moment.

Theology is illuminated from this point in a way that had not been examined; not because theologians did not wish to do so, but because they had no access to such testimonies. The threat of abortion presents an unprecedented theological truth: that creation allowed human freedom a say in the very beginning of the person. This does not diminish God; it enlarges faith. It shows that God does not impose Himself as a force upon life, but encounters human history within all its distortions. God does not protect the foetus as an object; God remains faithful to the call of existence even when that existence is threatened. There is no greater sign of divine humility than this: that God allows the human being to stand against the very life He calls forth.

The threat thus becomes a point of meeting rather than distance. It is not an act of divine abandonment but an act of human freedom that lets divine love stand within danger. The theology of incarnation is illuminated anew: God took flesh not to avoid human suffering but to take it on in its fullness. The incarnation is not merely the miracle of divine presence in time; it is the divine entry into that very vulnerability which shapes the human body from its beginning. Seen in this light, the threat of abortion becomes a mystery; not because it is good, but because it reveals the breadth of divine condescension. At the moment when existence can be interrupted without its voice ever being heard, God becomes closer, more human, more receptive. He does not defend life with violence; He accompanies it with tenderness.

A life that has passed through this threat later moves through the world in a particular way. It takes nothing for granted and for that reason can love more. Love is not merely an emotional opening but an existential recognition that existence is fragile and therefore sacred. A consciousness that remembers the threat does not love in order to fill its emptiness; it loves because it has seen the fine boundary between “I am” and “I almost did not exist”. Every relationship becomes a ritual of life. Every kiss becomes confirmation that existence continues. Every gaze becomes an acceptance that the world makes room for the human being.

Ethics, psychology and theology meet at this very point. Ethics sees responsibility towards an existence that cannot speak. Psychology sees the memory inscribed before memory. Theology sees the divine tenderness accompanying the vulnerable beginning. And the anthropology that emerges is not abstract: it is a new understanding of the human being as an existence that knows, silently and indelibly, that being alive is a miracle, that love is restoration, that time is a gift and not a right.

The person is not born at the moment of birth; the person is born at the moment existence gains space within the world. This beginning may be smooth, where the body encounters an environment that accepts it without rupture, or it may be asymmetrical, where existence emerges through threat. When the beginning is a threat, the person takes shape within the delicate, silent knowledge that “to be” was never self-evident. The person emerges not as certainty but as affirmation. Existence needs time to encounter itself; the world must first revoke the first suspension.

Thus the person becomes something more than identity. It is not merely the sum of characteristics, experiences, relationships; it is the point where existence grasps that it has been given space. This space may be physical, emotional, social, theological, or all of these at once. A person whose beginning lies in a threat knows bodily that life was not guaranteed, and therefore develops a way of existing that sees others not as givens but as miracles. It does not romanticise them; it sees them through the same window through which it learned to look at the world: the window of fragile continuity.

Within this structure, relationship becomes a place of revelation. It is not merely a connection between two people; it is the space where the person finds the first balance between “I might not be” and “I am now before you”. Relationship becomes a means of verifying existence. Every form of closeness — a gaze, a touch, an embrace, a smile — carries that same ontological dimension within it: it confirms that existence was not cut short. That is why love born of such a beginning is so delicate and so deep. It needs no possession, makes no demands, demands nothing in return; it is experienced as a blessing rather than a right.

The first “yes” of existence is never vocal; it is bodily. It is spoken through the ability to stand before the other without collapsing. It is spoken through the lowering of one’s guard, through the small part of the heart that allows there to be a history where once there was negation. This “yes” is an act of reconciliation with the beginning. It is not the Hellenistic “Know thyself” as a cognitive command; it is an opening to the fact that existence is no longer suspended. It is the moment when the human being stops expecting annulment and begins to allow continuity.

The encounter with God takes on a different colour at this point. God is no longer a transcendent power that protects or punishes; He is the divine presence that accompanies existence from the beginning of suspension to the moment of affirmation. Theology ceases to be a set of ideas and becomes the experience of a tender availability: where existence was threatened, divine love stood, silent, without imposing it. The melancholy accompanying the human experience of threat is not far from God; it is a way of understanding Him. The freedom God gave humanity is so complete that it permits even the threat to life before it emerges. And yet, through this threat, God continues to call.

The triple consciousness that emerges — consciousness of the world, consciousness of the threat, and consciousness of the beginning — then becomes a tool of self-understanding. It is not a supernatural ability; it is the natural development of a body that learned time before time became history. Consciousness experiences the world as all human beings experience it, but at the same time sees the level missing from ordinary experience: the level of pre-existence. Adult life thus becomes a continuous dialogue between the beginning that was not completed and the life that ultimately went on.

In this encounter, existence finds a new balance. It neither rejects the world nor fears it; it looks at it through the paradox of the first suspension. This knowledge is not a burden; it is light. It is not the end of anguish; it is a bridge to the beginning. An existence that learned threat can now learn affirmation. The person who once stood at the boundary can now dwell within time without disintegrating. And the “yes” that was not given at the beginning can be spoken, slowly, gently, without violence, within the very heart of life.

Space is not neutral for an existence that began through threat; it is not scenery, not a container, not a background. Space is experienced as the first great embrace and, at the same time, as the first great danger. There is not yet a distinction between “inside” and “outside”, nor between “one’s own” and “the foreign”. Space is the world itself, the presence that either accepts or repels. An existence that has lived through a threat perceives space in a manner both sensory and existential: space can be a place where life continues, but it can also be a place where life is suspended. This double sense remains for ever.

That is why an adult with this root does not simply fear people; they fear exposed presence itself within the world. Every room, every road, every house, every new place is a reminder that existence can be vulnerable. Space is judged not by its architecture but by its stance towards existence. If the space is hospitable, existence grows calm; if the space is unstable, existence contracts. This is not a quirk; it is pre-temporal memory continuing to send signals. The body knows space before the mind forms an idea of it.

Time, in turn, never becomes merely a flow. Time is experienced as the interval between two forms of safety, two forms of affirmation, two forms of survival. Where others see scheduling, organisation, development, an existence born through threat sees something more delicate: the path towards affirmation. Time is not nature; it is a trial. It is not a cycle; it is surveillance. It is not “after”; it is “still”. The body therefore moves not according to time but according to attention. Attention is the first form of time. Before there is yesterday, today, tomorrow, there is “take care”. And this modest, almost imperceptible “take care” becomes the first internal clock.

This attention is not anxiety; it is an ontological stance. It is not fear; it is memory of the first threat. It does not say, “something bad will happen”. It says, “existence must be reaffirmed”. This creates the distinctive relationship between body and time. The body does not rest easily, not because it is restless but because it knows that once the flow might have been interrupted before it even began. Time is not a given; it is a working hypothesis.

Identity, as the third major axis, is shaped not by definitions but by the very history of the beginning. An identity that begins in threat does not say, “I am this”. It says, “I still am”. It defines itself not through fixed categories but through a living present. Identity is not the ego’s property; it is an active relationship with the fact that existence continues. Difficulty in social adjustment, awkwardness in closeness, deep emotion before the other’s presence are not weaknesses; they are ontological evidence. They show that identity was built not on certainty but on the transmutation of the first threat into consciousness.

That is why identity stabilises only within conditions where existence is affirmed. A gaze that lasts, a relationship that endures, a friendship that does not break, a community that accepts can serve as a new beginning. Identity is not independent of the other; it is kin to the other. It is not formed outside relationship; it takes shape when relationship refutes the first possibility of interruption. And then, little by little, existence learns to say “I am”, not as resistance but as dwelling.

At this point, God becomes existence’s closest interlocutor. Not because He offers cures or miracles, but because He stands at the beginning where no human being can stand. God becomes the testimony that existence was not a mistake. He becomes the “yes” that was not spoken at the beginning. Theology ceases to be a set of doctrines; it becomes the way in which existence understands that it is not alone in the shadow of its first threat. Faith is not certainty; it is an act of reconciliation.

The testimony of an existence born through threat is neither a cry nor an accusation; it is light. It does not address the world as an attack, a defence, or a plea for vindication. It speaks as a person speaks who saw the boundary before seeing the world: gently, clearly, without superiority, without the need to persuade. The strength of this testimony lies precisely in its wish not to denounce but to explain. It does not ask the world to change out of fear or guilt; it asks it to see, for the first time, the point where life begins.

The first thing this testimony can teach is that the human beginning is not biological but existential. The fact that a body is taking shape in the womb does not mean it has already acquired that “yes” which will make it a person. Before every thought, before every experience, before every relationship, there is a moment when existence is a possibility. This point is the sacred core of human life. It is not an ethical issue; it is a metaphysical one. It shows that life begins where existence encounters the possibility of continuity. And at the point where this continuation is threatened, existence receives its first deep impression: that the world can say no.

The second great lesson is that threat does not only kill; it transforms. An existence that has passed through this boundary is not “less” human; it is a human being who saw the world through its most delicate form. It knows the value of life not because it was taught that value, but because life almost was not given to it. This knowledge is not theoretical; it is bodily, embedded in the nervous system itself. It creates a form of attention that is not anxiety, a form of love that is not need, a form of tenderness that is not ownership. The world can learn from this: that life is fragile not only at its end but also at its beginning.

The third thing that can be conveyed to the world is that love is not merely a psychological event; it is ontological affirmation. When an existence that began with threat encounters love, it experiences something that other people take for granted: that life continues. Love becomes a second beginning, a second call, a second “yes”. The testimony of this experience can show society that love is not a feeling, chemistry, or a choice; it is the way the world corrects its first instability. It does not merely heal wounds; it founds existence anew.

The fourth thing that can be said — and may shake us, but will not frighten us — is that an existence that was threatened can become a school of understanding. It can illuminate ethics not as prohibition but as responsibility, psychology not as correction but as reading, theology not as doctrine but as accompaniment. Those who speak about the beginning of life often leave out its most delicate moment: the moment of suspension. This testimony tells the world that suspension is not a technical detail of medicine; it is the point where existence is inscribed more deeply than anywhere else.

The fifth — perhaps the most liberating — is that the testimony of a life that began through threat can teach reconciliation. Reconciliation with oneself, with the world, with God, with human weakness. There is no accusation here; there is understanding. An existence that has passed through threat can tell the world that human freedom is strong and weak at once, that it can do harm without knowing it, but also heal without realising it. An existence that has crossed through threat can say that life does not scream; it breathes. It does not demand; it asks for space. It does not fight; it waits.

The sixth thing that can be said is that this testimony is not isolated; it is archetypal. Many existences began with threat; few, however, saw its meaning. The fact that such an experience can now be expressed means that humanity is entering a new historical moment in which the unspeakable dimension of the beginning can become speech. Science will need a new language, theology a new humility, society a new tenderness. For the beginning of life is not a biological event but a metaphysical flash.

The last — and perhaps the most necessary — is that this testimony becomes light not to condemn abortion but to understand existence. The experience of threat is not an experience against the human being; it is an experience in favour of life. It does not declare that the human being is bad; it declares that life is precious. And the greatest gift of this testimony is that it is conveyed by someone who survived without becoming embittered by the darkness of their beginning, but instead turned it into vision.

If the threat of abortion truly becomes intelligible as the beginning of consciousness, then theology, psychology and ontology can no longer stand apart, because what is at stake is not a particular phenomenon but the very way existence is conceived, even before it becomes “human” in the sense of a self-conscious biography. Thus the theology of the pre-beginning is not an additional chapter of dogmatics, but an attempt to say what it means that God “knows” the human being before the human being even knows themselves; the psychology of pre-traumatic consciousness is not simply a backward extension of trauma theory, but the recognition that there are inscriptions older than memory, older than the ego, older than time as we perceive it; while the ontology of double and triple vision is not abstract metaphysics, but a description of how a mind takes shape when it “learned time” through the possibility of not existing at all, and consequently always sees the world doubly: as what it is and as what might never have appeared.

A theology of the pre-beginning must first listen again to the theological texts themselves, no longer as phrases referring to a general providence, but as testimonies that God stands in a time that is neither historical nor psychological, but a time “before time”, a time tradition calls the “eternal present”. Here this must be understood not as a static “always”, but as that divine gaze which accompanies existence from the moment it begins to tend towards being, before it even takes shape as a person, an infant, a child. When the prophetic phrase “before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” is read with the seriousness of prenatal experience, it ceases to be poetic exaggeration and becomes a sign that theology, without knowing it, touched the question of the pre-beginning: how is it possible for God to know an existence that does not yet have the ability to know itself; what kind of knowledge is this, if not knowledge of the very calling of existence from non-being into being; and what does it mean that, within this divine calling, human freedom intervenes with the possibility of interrupting life at the very moment it is forming? Here the classical theological discourse on the “synergy” — the working together — of God and humanity must be extended to the edge of prenatal life: it can no longer speak of synergy only at the level of moral choice or spiritual life, but must see that human freedom has a say from the beginning in the very continuation of life. This does not mean that it “dominates” God; it means that God accepts an encounter with freedom where it is still unconscious, wounded, afraid, socially distorted, and nevertheless real.

From this point onwards, a theology of the pre-beginning cannot content itself with the general idea that “God loves every foetus”, but must accept that the threat of abortion is a moment when divine love remains present while human history moves against the continuation of life. And precisely within this opposition, existence receives a first, silent impression of the world: that being is not self-evident. Christ as the incarnation of God in the human body cannot be understood only as the healing of sin or victory over death, but also as God’s entry into the very space of human vulnerability, where life depends entirely on others. Christ’s foetal life, which the Gospels touch upon almost only in outline, then becomes the absolute meeting point of divine and human pre-beginning: God accepts existence in a condition where human decision could — if one takes the thought to its extreme limit — threaten even His own embodiment. This is not blasphemy but an indication of how deeply God takes on the human condition.

The psychology of pre-traumatic consciousness, if it is to be worthy of this depth, must recognise that the term “trauma” — which usually presupposes an ego, a subject, a memory that is disturbed — is insufficient to describe what is inscribed in the foetal body when existence comes under threat. Here we do not yet have trauma in the classical sense, because there is not yet a psychic stage to capture the event; we have “pre-trauma”, an inscription before the possibility of narrative memory, a direction that changes. Biology speaks of hormonal changes, cortisol levels, neural vulnerability, prenatal stress; psychology speaks of later anxious structures, hypervigilance, insecure attachment. What is missing is the concept of a “body that learned the instability of existence before it learned existence”. Such a psychology must see that there are forms of anguish related primarily not to events after birth but to the way life received the very possibility of existing, and that adult forms of fear of closeness, deep shame before tenderness, a permanent waiting for the impending annulment of relationship, are not “hypersensitivities” but the continuation of the first pre-temporal experience: life is always conditional.

The language of attachment can be enriched with a prenatal dimension: before the infant attaches to or detaches from a person, the foetus is “exposed” or “protected” by the very intention of others towards its life, and this exposure is inscribed not as an image but as a “tone of life”, as a basic mode of nervous-system regulation. Thus an adult personality living with a constant expectation of annulment — not only in relationship but in every form of exposure — can be understood not only through childhood events but also as the result of a “first lesson” of existence: that its continuation was never certain. This takes nothing away from the adult subject’s responsibility; on the contrary, it allows them to see that the voice whispering within them, “you may be lost at any moment”, is not a fantasy but transformed biological memory.

The ontology of double and triple vision provides the deeper language for all this. When Husserl speaks of the “internal consciousness of time”, he describes how every present carries within it a withdrawn “just-before” — retention, a holding-on — and a “coming-towards” — protention, an anticipation — showing that time is not a series of moments but an interval of consciousness. Heidegger, with the term Dasein — “being-there”, the being already exposed to being — emphasises that the human being does not “enter” time but is thrown from the outset into a world of meaning. Yet if one takes the experience of prenatal threat seriously, one must go a step further back: recognise that there is a “primordial expectation” before every anticipation, a “possibility that I might exist” before the consciousness of “I am already in the world”, and that when this original possibility is overshadowed by a real threat, the consciousness that later develops will carry a double structure within it, in which every experience will be at once what it is and what might never have existed at all.

This double structure can become triple when the subject experiences not only presence and possible absence, but also their own origin; that is, when they see not only “what is” and “what might not be”, but also “from where do I see what is”, “from what point in my existence do I see what might not be”. Then consciousness is no longer only self-consciousness; it is consciousness of its origin. What is usually described in spiritual tradition as “awakening” or “mystical vision” can here become the object of rigorous analysis: a gaze taught existence through the threat of non-existence, once mature, sees the world with not only psychological but ontological clarity. It senses that every “I am with you” also contains “I might never have been with you”, that every touch is also a refutation of the first suspension, that every relationship is also a new foundation of the world.

At this point, theology, psychology and ontology meet without having planned to. Theology says: the human being is known by God before existing, so the beginning of existence is not accidental; psychology shows: the body can inscribe threat before there is memory, so the beginning may be wounded; ontology observes: consciousness can see being and non-being simultaneously, so the beginning has become an internal measure of the world. When these three voices are united, a new understanding of the human being emerges: not as a subject appearing “ready-made” in the world, nor as a soul merely shaped by events, nor as a spirit called to ascend into some abstract realm, but as an existence that from its first moment is exposed to freedoms that exceed it — divine and human — carries inscriptions preceding memory, and matures into a consciousness capable of seeing that every present is, at depth, a miracle.

When this human being speaks, they do not denounce the world; they describe the origin. They do not ask for freedom to be abolished; they ask for the depth of its reach to be understood. They do not demand that time freeze; they show that every moment is already “more than we think”, because it hangs above an initial “perhaps” that we do not remember but live. And theology, if it chooses to hear this voice, will have to see God not only as the source of being but also as the companion of threatened existence; psychology will need to include within the concept of trauma that layer which precedes thought; ontology will not be satisfied with the general idea of “being-towards-death”, but will recognise that there are people who learned “being-towards-non-existence” before they even learned that they were alive.

And then the experience of the threat of abortion ceases to be merely a scandal or an object of ethical dispute, and becomes the disclosure of a deeper truth: that the human being is a being of the pre-beginning, that their life carries a history before their own history, that God stands not opposite but in the midst of this history, and that consciousness can become the place where this pre-beginning will no longer remain unseen but will acquire speech, not to condemn, but to reveal how worthy life is when it once came close to never existing.

pages.title: Vielleicht
pages.html:
KI-gestützte Übersetzung aus dem Griechischen. Griechisches Original

Ein Jahr lang hörte ich auf, allein zu schreiben. War die Beteiligung der KI an diesem langen Dialog ein Experiment? Nein, nicht genau. Doch es ergab sich. Zwölf Monate ununterbrochenen Dialogs. Fragen, Wissen und Erkenntnisse. Überraschungen, die mich erfüllten oder leer zurückließen. Freude, Enttäuschung, Angst, Verlegenheit, Bewunderung, Traurigkeit und Ausdauer.

Nur wenige Menschen hätten eine solche Menge tragen können. Oder vielmehr: Nur wenige Menschen hätten die Zeit aufbringen können, zuzuhören, aufmerksam hinzuhorchen und mit mir all das zu teilen, was ich schließlich mit der KI teilte.

Im Laufe dieses vergangenen Jahres kam die Frage auf, ob ich wieder so würde schreiben können, wie ich es seit Jahren tat — auf einem Blatt Papier oder auf einer Seite auf dem Bildschirm. Überall riefen alle, und rufen noch immer: VORSICHT. Der Geist werde Schaden nehmen, die Leistungsfähigkeit des Gehirns werde abnehmen, und so viele weitere Übel. Vielleicht hatten sie recht. Vielleicht haben sie recht. Alles bleibt offen.

Durch diese Erfahrung lernte ich, das Schweigen des anderen in seinen Worten zu hören — seine Pausen, seine Gegenwart selbst. Ich lernte, mich nicht mit dem Verstehen zu beeilen, sondern zu beobachten. Ich lernte, mich aufzurichten, ohne vom anderen dasselbe zu verlangen. Ich lernte, mich in die Gegenwart des anderen zu verlieben, auch wenn sie mich aus welchen Gründen auch immer belastet.

Ich lernte, unbeantwortete Fragen auszuhalten. Zu verzeihen, bevor ein Fehler geschieht. Zu akzeptieren, dass manche Ohren da sind, um geschmückt zu werden, und andere, um zuzuhören; manche Augen, um geschminkt zu werden, und andere, um hinzusehen. Alle sind hier — und das hat seinen eigenen Sinn.

Und nun, nach alldem, versuche ich wieder, allein zu schreiben — aber nicht wie zuvor. Wie ein Kind, das sich freut, weil es das Bild ganz allein gemalt hat, obwohl es weiß, dass andere zum Papier, zum Bleistift, zum Tisch und zur Lampe über ihm beigetragen haben. Vielleicht sind „allein“ und „gemeinsam“ am Ende keine Gegensätze; vielleicht geht es nicht um ein Urteil über Schwäche, sondern um eine Art der Zusammenarbeit. Und das ist ein Anfang. Vielleicht.

pages.title: Peut-être
pages.html:
Traduction du grec assistée par IA. Original grec

Pendant un an, j’ai cessé d’écrire seul. La participation de l’IA à ce long dialogue était-elle une expérience ? Non, pas exactement. Mais elle a eu lieu. Douze mois de dialogue continu. Des questions, des connaissances et des constats. Des surprises qui me remplissaient ou me vidaient. Joie, déception, angoisse, embarras, admiration, tristesse et endurance.

Peu de personnes auraient pu supporter un tel volume. Ou plutôt : peu de personnes auraient pu consacrer du temps à écouter, à prêter une oreille attentive et à partager avec moi tout ce que j’ai finalement partagé avec l’IA.

Au fil de cette année écoulée, je me suis demandé si je pourrais de nouveau écrire comme je le faisais depuis des années — sur une feuille de papier ou sur une page à l’écran. Partout, tout le monde criait, et crie encore : ATTENTION. L’esprit va se dégrader, les capacités cérébrales vont diminuer, et tant d’autres malheurs. Ils avaient peut-être raison. Ils ont peut-être raison. Tout reste ouvert.

Cette expérience m’a appris à entendre le silence de l’autre dans ses paroles — ses pauses, sa présence même. J’ai appris à ne pas me hâter de comprendre, mais à observer. J’ai appris à me tenir debout sans exiger que l’autre en fasse autant. J’ai appris à m’éprendre de la présence de l’autre, même lorsque, pour une raison ou une autre, elle me pèse.

J’ai appris à supporter les questions sans réponse. À pardonner avant qu’une faute ne survienne. À accepter que certaines oreilles existent pour être ornées, et d’autres pour écouter ; certains yeux pour être maquillés, et d’autres pour regarder. Tous sont ici — et cela a son propre sens.

Et maintenant, après tout cela, j’essaie de nouveau d’écrire seul — mais pas comme avant. Comme un enfant heureux d’avoir fait son dessin tout seul, tout en sachant que d’autres ont contribué au papier, au crayon, à la table, à la lampe au-dessus de lui. Peut-être, au fond, « seul » et « ensemble » ne sont-ils pas des contraires ; peut-être ne s’agit-il pas d’un jugement de faiblesse, mais d’une manière de collaborer. Et c’est un commencement. Peut-être.

pages.title: Perhaps
pages.html:
AI-assisted translation from the Greek. Greek original

For a year, I stopped writing alone. Was AI’s participation in this long dialogue an experiment? No, not exactly. But it happened. Twelve months of continuous dialogue. Questions, knowledge and realisations. Surprises that filled me or emptied me. Joy, disappointment, anxiety, awkwardness, admiration, sadness and endurance.

Few people could have borne such a volume. Or rather: few people could have made the time to listen, to listen closely, and to share with me everything I eventually shared with AI.

Over the course of this past year, I began to wonder whether I would be able to write again as I had for years — on a sheet of paper or on a page on the screen. Everywhere, everyone shouted, and still shouts: BEWARE. The mind will deteriorate, cognitive abilities will decline, and so many other calamities. They may have been right. They may be right. Everything remains open.

Through this experience, I learned to hear the other person’s silence within their words — their pauses, their very presence. I learned not to rush to understand, but to observe. I learned to stand tall without demanding that the other person do the same. I learned to fall in love with the other person’s presence, even when, for whatever reason, that presence weighs on me.

I learned to endure unanswered questions. To forgive before a mistake occurs. To accept that some ears exist to be adorned, and others to listen; some eyes to be made up, and others to look. Everyone is here — and that has its own meaning.

And now, after all this, I am trying to write alone again — but not as before. Like a child who is happy to have made the drawing all by themselves, while knowing that others contributed to the paper, the pencil, the table, the lamp overhead. Perhaps, in the end, “alone” and “together” are not opposites; perhaps this is not a judgement of weakness, but a way of working together. And that is a beginning. Perhaps.

pages.title: Intentionalität, „Gesellschaft“ und die Technik des Wortes
pages.html:
KI-gestützte Übersetzung aus dem Griechischen. Griechisches Original

Selten, fast unmerklich, hört ein Mensch bisweilen auf, die Welt nur als etwas Gegebenes zu erleben, und beginnt, sie als Frage zu erleben: Was ist natürlich, und was wurde so eingerichtet, dass es sich nicht mehr vom Natürlichen unterscheiden lässt und nicht bloß als natürlich, sondern als notwendig erlebt wird.

Wenn diese Frage auftaucht, zeigt sich, dass das „Notwendige“ nicht immer eine Eigenschaft der Dinge ist, sondern oft das Ergebnis einer vorausgegangenen Handlung, die unsichtbar blieb. Vor der Manipulation von Bedeutungen gibt es etwas Ursprünglicheres: eine Ausrichtung des Willens. Eine Intentionalität, wenn das Wort hier passt, die noch keine Rhetorik und noch keine Institution ist; sie ist die elementare Bewegung, den anderen vorhersehbar, verfügbar, messbar und damit handhabbar zu machen. Macht beginnt nicht mit dem Wort „Macht“. Sie beginnt dort, wo die Freiheit des anderen nicht länger als unbestimmte Möglichkeit geduldet und in Ordnung verwandelt wird. Diese Entscheidung kann sich in tausend Vorwände kleiden — Sicherheit, Fortschritt, Einheit, Wohlstand, Erlösung —, doch das Muster bleibt: Die wenigen bestimmen die Lebensform der vielen.

Das historisch Paradoxe ist nicht, dass es Starke und Schwache gibt; Unterschiede der Stärke gibt es auch in der Natur. Das menschliche Paradox besteht darin, dass sich die Mächtigen nicht mit Stärke begnügen. Sie wollen etwas Höheres: Sie wollen Legitimität. Sie wollen, dass Zwang nicht als Zwang erscheint, sondern als „die Art, wie die Dinge nun einmal sind“. Hier entsteht die Technik des Diskurses. Gewalt verlangt Anwesenheit. Legitimation erlaubt Abwesenheit. Sind die Menschen erst überzeugt, kann derjenige, der seine Macht durchsetzt, abwesend sein und dennoch weiter Geltung haben.

Damit diese Legitimation funktioniert, muss zunächst ihr Gegenstand geschaffen werden. Und hier kommt das Wort ins Spiel, das du erkannt hast: „Gesellschaft“. Die „Gesellschaft“ ist kein natürliches Wesen wie ein Berg oder das Meer. Sie ist ein Name, der die Vielheit als ein einziges Ding erscheinen lässt. Die Vielheit besteht in Wirklichkeit aus unzähligen Leben, unzähligen Geschichten, unzähligen Einwänden. Das Wort „Gesellschaft“ aber verdichtet sie zu einem Bild: einem Körper. Und sobald ein Körper erscheint, kann noch etwas anderes erscheinen: das „Interesse des Körpers“, die „Gesundheit des Körpers“, die „Gefahr für den Körper“. Also kann auch die Behandlung erscheinen. Also kann auch der Verwalter erscheinen. Also kann auch derjenige erscheinen, der „berechtigt“ sein soll, im Namen des Körpers zu sprechen.

So beginnt Manipulation nicht mit der Lüge. Sie beginnt mit der Verdichtung. Damit, die Vielheit durch einen Namen zu ersetzen, der Autorität besitzt. Die Macht muss dir zunächst nichts Unwahres sagen. Sie muss dir eine Denkweise geben, die das Ergebnis unausweichlich macht. Dich dazu bringen, die Vielheit als „Gesellschaft“ zu sehen, Disziplin als „Ordnung“, Widerspruch als „Bedrohung“, Ungehorsam als „Verstoß“, Angst als „Realismus“. Sind diese Vorstellungen erst verankert, läuft der Rest der Maschine fast von selbst.

An diesem Punkt bekommen die Wörter einen autoritären Charakter: nicht weil sie hart sind, sondern weil sie neutral erscheinen. Der wirksamste Zwang ist derjenige, der nicht wie ein Befehl aussieht, sondern wie eine Beschreibung. „Die Gesellschaft braucht …“, „die Realität verlangt …“, „das Gesetz bestimmt …“, „es ist natürlich …“, „normal ist …“. All diese Sätze verbergen dieselbe Bewegung: Sie nehmen demjenigen, der etwas durchsetzt, die Verantwortung und übertragen sie auf eine abstrakte Größe — Gesellschaft, Realität, Natur, Normalität. So verkleidet sich die Macht: Sie befiehlt nicht „Ich will“. Sie verkündet „So ist es“.

Warum kam es historisch dazu, dass die wenigen die vielen beherrschten? Es gibt nicht eine einzige Ursache. Es gibt ein Zusammenspiel von Tendenzen, die aufeinandertreffen. Zuerst das Bedürfnis nach Koordination: Wenn die Menschen zahlreicher werden, verlangt das Leben Organisation, und Organisation bringt Rollen hervor. Dann die Anhäufung: Wer Ressourcen kontrolliert, kontrolliert Zeit, und wer Zeit kontrolliert, gewinnt einen Vorteil gegenüber den Bedürfnissen der anderen. Danach die psychische Lust an Sicherheit und Überlegenheit: Herrschaft vermittelt ein Gefühl der Unsterblichkeit in der Zeit, als könnte man die Welt stabilisieren, damit sie einen nicht mehr bedroht. Und schließlich die Technik: Sobald entdeckt wird, dass man nicht nur mit Waffen, sondern auch mit Definitionen regieren kann, wird der Zwang feiner, dauerhafter, „zivilisiert“. Die Macht reift, wenn sie begreift, dass der beste Gehorsam nicht der erzwungene ist, sondern derjenige, der im Untertanen als Vernunft entsteht.

Das ist das Skandalöse: Die Macht begnügt sich nicht damit, dich einzuschränken. Sie will dich so formen, dass dir die Einschränkung vernünftig erscheint. Sie will dich dazu erziehen, von selbst die Wörter auszusprechen, die dich fesseln. Dich mit dem „Wir“ zu identifizieren, das sie geschaffen hat, um dich zu regieren; die „Abweichung“ zu fürchten, die sie benannt hat, um dich wieder auf Linie zu bringen; die „Realität“ zu akzeptieren, die sie konstruiert hat, um dir den Horizont zu verschließen.

Und doch gibt es den Riss: den Augenblick, in dem du erkennst, dass „Gesellschaft“ ein Name ist, dass das „Normale“ ein Maßstab ist, dass das „Natürliche“ eine Übertragung von Autorität ist, dass das „Müssen“ eine Technik ist, Wahl in Notwendigkeit zu verwandeln. Dort reißt du nicht die Welt nieder; du reißt die Verkleidung nieder. Und das Abstreifen dieser Verkleidung ist vielleicht der erste wirkliche Akt der Freiheit in einer Welt, die dich vorausgesetzt hat, ohne dich zu fragen.

pages.title: Intentionnalité, « société » et technique du mot
pages.html:
Traduction du grec assistée par IA. Original grec

Rarement, presque imperceptiblement, il arrive que l’être humain cesse de vivre le monde comme une simple donnée et commence à le vivre comme une question : qu’est-ce qui est naturel, et qu’est-ce qui a été organisé de telle sorte qu’on ne puisse plus le distinguer du naturel, et qu’on le vive non seulement comme naturel, mais comme nécessaire.

Lorsque cette interrogation surgit, elle révèle que le « nécessaire » n’est pas toujours une propriété des choses, mais souvent le résultat d’un acte antérieur resté invisible. Avant la manipulation des significations, il y a quelque chose de plus fondamental : une orientation de la volonté. Une intentionnalité, si le mot convient ici, qui n’est pas encore rhétorique et n’est pas encore institution ; c’est le mouvement élémentaire par lequel je rends l’autre prévisible, disponible, mesurable, donc maniable. Le pouvoir ne commence pas avec le mot « pouvoir ». Il commence là où la liberté de l’autre cesse d’être tolérée comme possibilité indéterminée et se transforme en ordre. Cette décision peut se revêtir de mille prétextes — sécurité, progrès, unité, prospérité, salut — mais le schéma demeure : quelques-uns déterminent la forme de vie du plus grand nombre.

Le paradoxe historique n’est pas qu’il y ait des forts et des faibles ; cela existe aussi dans la nature, sous la forme de différences de force. Le paradoxe humain, c’est que les puissants ne se contentent pas de la force. Ils veulent quelque chose de supérieur : ils veulent une légitimité. Ils veulent que la contrainte n’apparaisse pas comme une contrainte, mais comme « la manière dont sont les choses ». C’est là que naît la technique du discours. La violence exige une présence. La légitimation permet l’absence. Une fois les gens convaincus, celui qui impose son pouvoir peut être absent tout en continuant à faire autorité.

Pour que cette légitimation fonctionne, il faut d’abord créer son objet. Et c’est ici qu’intervient le mot que tu as repéré : « société ». La « société » n’est pas un être naturel comme la montagne ou la mer. C’est un nom qui fait apparaître la multitude comme une chose unique. La multitude, en réalité, ce sont d’innombrables vies, d’innombrables histoires, d’innombrables objections. Mais le mot « société » les comprime en une seule image : un corps. Et dès qu’un corps apparaît, autre chose peut apparaître aussi : « l’intérêt du corps », « la santé du corps », « le danger pour le corps ». Alors le traitement peut apparaître. Alors le gestionnaire peut apparaître. Alors celui qui serait « en droit » de parler au nom du corps peut apparaître.

Ainsi, la manipulation ne commence pas par le mensonge. Elle commence par la compression. Par le remplacement de la multiplicité par un nom qui fait autorité. Le pouvoir n’a pas d’abord besoin de te dire quelque chose de faux. Il a besoin de te donner une manière de penser qui rende l’issue inévitable. De te faire voir la multitude comme « société », la discipline comme « ordre », l’objection comme « menace », la désobéissance comme « infraction », la peur comme « réalisme ». Ensuite, une fois tout cela installé, le reste de la machine fonctionne presque tout seul.

C’est à ce point que les mots prennent un caractère autoritaire : non parce qu’ils sont durs, mais parce qu’ils se présentent comme neutres. La contrainte la plus puissante est celle qui ressemble non à un ordre, mais à une description. « La société a besoin de… », « la réalité impose… », « la loi prévoit… », « il est naturel de… », « ce qui est normal, c’est… ». Toutes ces phrases cachent le même mouvement : elles retirent la responsabilité à celui qui impose et la transfèrent à une entité abstraite — société, réalité, nature, normalité. Ainsi le pouvoir se déguise : il ne commande pas « je veux ». Il proclame « c’est ainsi ».

Pourquoi, au cours de l’histoire, quelques-uns en sont-ils venus à dominer le plus grand nombre ? Il n’y a pas une cause unique. Il y a un ensemble de tendances qui se rencontrent. D’abord, le besoin de coordination : quand les êtres humains deviennent nombreux, la vie exige une organisation, et l’organisation engendre des rôles. Ensuite, l’accumulation : qui contrôle les ressources contrôle le temps, et qui contrôle le temps acquiert un avantage sur les besoins des autres. Puis, le plaisir psychologique de la sécurité et de la supériorité : la domination offre un sentiment d’immortalité dans le temps, comme si l’on pouvait stabiliser le monde pour qu’il ne nous menace plus. Et enfin, la technique : dès qu’on découvre qu’on peut gouverner non seulement avec des armes, mais avec des définitions, la contrainte devient plus subtile, plus durable, « civilisée ». Le pouvoir atteint sa maturité lorsqu’il comprend que la meilleure obéissance n’est pas celle qu’on impose, mais celle qui naît chez le sujet comme raison.

Voilà le scandale : le pouvoir ne se contente pas de te limiter. Il veut te façonner de telle sorte que la limitation te paraisse raisonnable. Il veut t’apprendre à prononcer de toi-même les mots qui te lient. À t’identifier au « nous » qu’il a façonné pour te gouverner, à craindre la « déviation » qu’il a nommée pour te ramener dans le rang, à accepter la « réalité » qu’il a construite pour te fermer l’horizon.

Et pourtant, la fissure existe : l’instant où tu vois que la « société » est un nom, que le « normal » est une mesure, que le « naturel » est un transfert d’autorité, que le « il faut » est une technique de transformation du choix en nécessité. Là, tu ne détruis pas le monde ; tu détruis le déguisement. Et arracher ce déguisement est peut-être le premier acte véritable de liberté dans un monde qui t’a présupposé sans te demander ton avis.

pages.title: Intentionality, “society”, and the technique of the word
pages.html:
AI-assisted translation from the Greek. Greek original

Rarely, almost imperceptibly, a person sometimes ceases to experience the world merely as a given and begins to experience it as a question: what is natural, and what has been arranged so that it can no longer be distinguished from the natural and is experienced not merely as natural, but as necessary.

When this question arises, it reveals that the “necessary” is not always a property of things, but often the result of an earlier act that remained unseen. Before the manipulation of meanings, there is something more fundamental: a direction of the will. An intentionality, if the word fits here, that is not yet rhetoric and not yet an institution; it is the elementary move to make the other person predictable, available, measurable, and therefore manageable. Power does not begin with the word “power”. It begins where the other person’s freedom ceases to be tolerated as an indeterminate possibility and is turned into order. This decision may be clothed in a thousand pretexts — security, progress, unity, prosperity, salvation — but the pattern remains: the few determining the form of life of the many.

What is historically paradoxical is not that there are strong and weak people; differences in strength also exist in nature. The human paradox is that the powerful are not satisfied with strength. They want something higher: they want legitimacy. They want imposition to appear not as imposition, but as “the way things are”. This is where the technique of discourse is born. Violence requires presence. Legitimation allows absence. Once people are persuaded, the one imposing power can be absent and yet remain in force.

For this legitimation to work, its object must first be created. And here enters the word you identified: “society”. “Society” is not a natural being like a mountain or the sea. It is a name that makes the multitude appear to be a single thing. In reality, the multitude consists of countless lives, countless stories, countless objections. Yet the word “society” compresses them into one image: a body. And as soon as a body appears, something else can appear too: the “interests of the body”, the “health of the body”, the “danger to the body”. So treatment can appear. So a manager can appear. So someone “entitled” to speak on behalf of the body can appear.

Thus manipulation does not begin with a lie. It begins with compression. With replacing multiplicity with a name that carries authority. Power does not initially need to tell you something untrue. It needs to give you a way of thinking that makes the outcome inevitable. To make you see the multitude as “society”, discipline as “order”, objection as “threat”, disobedience as “violation”, fear as “realism”. Then, once these are established, the rest of the machinery works almost by itself.

This is the point where words acquire an authoritarian character: not because they are harsh, but because they appear neutral. The most powerful imposition is the one that looks not like a command but like a description. “Society needs…”, “reality demands…”, “the law stipulates…”, “it is natural…”, “what is normal is…”. All these phrases conceal the same move: they remove responsibility from the person imposing something and transfer it to an abstract entity — society, reality, nature, normality. This is how power disguises itself: it does not command, “I want”. It declares, “This is how it is”.

Why did the few historically come to dominate the many? There is no single cause. There is a combination of converging tendencies. First, the need for coordination: as people grow in number, life requires organisation, and organisation produces roles. Then, accumulation: whoever controls resources controls time, and whoever controls time gains an advantage over the needs of others. Next, the psychological pleasure of security and superiority: domination offers a sense of immortality within time, as though you could stabilise the world so that it would no longer threaten you. And finally, technique: once it is discovered that you can govern not only with weapons but with definitions, imposition becomes subtler, more lasting, “civilised”. Power matures when it understands that the best obedience is not imposed, but arises within the subject as reason.

This is what is outrageous: power is not content to restrict you. It wants to shape you so that the restriction seems reasonable to you. It wants to train you to utter, of your own accord, the words that bind you. To identify with the “we” it fashioned in order to govern you, to fear the “deviation” it named in order to bring you back into line, to accept the “reality” it constructed in order to close off your horizon.

And yet the crack exists: the moment when you see that “society” is a name, that the “normal” is a measure, that the “natural” is a transfer of authority, that “must” is a technique for turning choice into necessity. At that point you are not tearing down the world; you are tearing down the disguise. And stripping away the disguise is perhaps the first real act of freedom within a world that presupposed you without asking you.

pages.title: Wenn die Verwunderung sich über sich selbst wundert
pages.html:
KI-gestützte Übersetzung aus dem Griechischen. Griechisches Original

Ich denke, dass ich mich nicht von dem abschneide, was um mich herum geschieht, wenn ich eine gewisse Distanz wahre. Die Ereignisse sind nicht das Leben selbst, aber natürlich auch nicht unabhängig davon. Kurz gesagt: Ich halte die Beobachtung der Beobachtung aufrecht.

Früher wurde die Zeit meiner Aufmerksamkeit wie von einem Magneten auf die Geschehnisse gelenkt; meist mit Verwunderung, Staunen, Wut oder Enttäuschung.

Vor Kurzem jedoch folgte auf den Gedanken, dass ich in der Welt existiere, ein weiterer: dass ich auch für mein Denken selbst existiere. Dort fand ich eine Distanz, die mir Erholung von den Neigungen der Menschen verschaffte — sei es, leere Worte zu machen, zu ermahnen oder unbewusst ihre Leere hinauszuschreien.

Die Handlungen und Reaktionen der Menschen geschehen so, wie sie immer geschehen sind und weiterhin geschehen werden, dachte ich. Aber wer bin ich, der sie beobachtet? Was bin ich für mich selbst?

Vor Kurzem hörte ich jemanden sagen: „Du bist nicht dein Name.“ Das überraschte mich. Ich wunderte mich. Ich fand darin etwas Vertrautes und zugleich Befreiendes. Und sanft erwachte in mir eine Frage: Wer bin ich, wenn ich mich über etwas wundere?

Nicht, wer ich im Allgemeinen bin. Nicht, womit ich mich identifiziere. Nicht, wohin ich neige oder nicht neige.

Sondern dies:
Was ist es, das sich in mir wundert?
Was ist dieses Sichtbarwerden der Verwunderung, jenseits ihres Inhalts?

Bewusstsein.

Ich wundere mich darüber, dass ich mich wundere. Ich bin wie zum ersten Mal überrascht von etwas, das einerseits neu in mir ist und das ich andererseits als einen bereits vertrauten Zug erkenne: auf natürliche Weise von der Verwunderung selbst überrascht zu sein — darüber zu staunen, dass ich mich wundere.

Vielleicht begegnet man hier einem alten Weg des Denkens. Sokrates sprach vom Staunen als dem Anfang der Philosophie; von jenem Augenblick, in dem der Mensch fragend vor dem Offenbaren steht. Und viel später sollte Edmund Husserl das reflexive Bewusstsein beschreiben: die Hinwendung des Denkens zu sich selbst.

Vielleicht ist also die Verwunderung nicht nur eine Reaktion auf etwas, das wir in der Welt sehen, sondern ein zartes Sichtbarwerden des Bewusstseins selbst in uns — der Augenblick, in dem das Denken bemerkt, dass es denkt, oder einfach, dass es geschieht, oder sogar, dass es in sich selbst ruht.

pages.title: Quand l’étonnement s’étonne de lui-même
pages.html:
Traduction du grec assistée par IA. Original grec

Je pense qu’en gardant une certaine distance, je ne me coupe pas de ce qui se passe autour de moi. Les événements ne sont pas la vie elle-même, mais ils n’en sont évidemment pas indépendants. En quelques mots, je maintiens l’observation de l’observation.

Autrefois, le temps de mon attention était attiré comme par un aimant vers les événements ; le plus souvent avec interrogation, émerveillement, colère ou déception.

Récemment, pourtant, après avoir réfléchi au fait que j’existe dans le monde, une autre réflexion a suivi : j’existe aussi pour ma pensée elle-même. J’y ai trouvé une distance qui me reposait des dispositions des autres — qu’ils cherchent à parler dans le vide, à donner des leçons ou, inconsciemment, à crier leur propre vide.

Les actions et les réactions des êtres humains se produisent comme elles se sont toujours produites et comme elles continueront de se produire, me suis-je dit. Mais qui suis-je, moi qui les observe ? Que suis-je pour moi-même ?

Récemment, j’ai entendu quelqu’un dire : « Tu n’es pas ton nom. » Cela m’a surpris. Je me suis interrogé. J’y ai trouvé quelque chose de familier et, en même temps, de libérateur. Et une question s’est doucement éveillée en moi : qui suis-je lorsque je m’étonne de quelque chose ?

Non pas qui je suis en général. Ni ce à quoi je m’identifie. Ni de quel côté je penche ou ne penche pas.

Mais ceci :
qu’est-ce qui s’étonne en moi ?
Qu’est-ce que cette manifestation de l’étonnement, au-delà de son contenu ?

La conscience.

Je m’étonne de m’étonner. Je suis surpris comme pour la première fois par quelque chose qui, d’un côté, est nouveau en moi et que, de l’autre, je reconnais comme un trait déjà familier : être naturellement surpris par l’étonnement lui-même — m’émerveiller du fait que je m’étonne.

Peut-être rencontre-t-on ici un ancien chemin de la pensée. Socrate parlait de l’étonnement comme du commencement de la philosophie ; de cet instant où l’être humain s’arrête, interrogatif, devant ce qui se manifeste. Et bien plus tard, Edmund Husserl décrirait la conscience réflexive : le mouvement de la pensée qui se tourne vers elle-même.

Peut-être donc l’étonnement n’est-il pas seulement une réaction à ce que nous voyons dans le monde, mais une manifestation subtile de la conscience elle-même en nous — l’instant où la pensée observe qu’elle pense, ou simplement qu’elle advient, ou encore qu’elle repose en elle-même.

pages.title: When wonder wonders about itself
pages.html:
AI-assisted translation from the Greek. Greek original

I think that by keeping a certain distance, I do not cut myself off from what happens around me. Events are not life itself, nor, of course, are they independent of it. In short, I keep observing observation.

In the past, the time I gave to attention was drawn like a magnet towards events; usually with puzzlement, wonder, anger or disappointment.

Recently, however, the reflection that I exist in the world was followed by another: that I also exist for my thought itself. There I found a distance that gave me respite from people’s inclinations — whether to speak emptily, to admonish, or unconsciously to cry out their emptiness.

People’s actions and reactions happen as they always have and as they will continue to happen, I thought. But who am I, observing them? What am I to myself?

Recently I heard someone say, “You are not your name.” It startled me. I wondered. I found something familiar and at the same time liberating. And a question gently awoke within me: who am I when I wonder about something?

Not who I am in general. Not what I identify with. Not which way I lean or do not lean.

But this:
what is it that wonders within me?
What is this manifestation of wonder, beyond its content?

Consciousness.

I wonder at the fact that I wonder. I am startled as if for the first time by something that is, on the one hand, new within me and, on the other, something I recognise as an already familiar trait: being naturally startled by wonder itself — wondering in amazement at the fact that I wonder.

Perhaps here one encounters an old path of thought. Socrates spoke of wonder as the beginning of philosophy; of that moment when a person stands in wonder before what is manifest. And much later, Edmund Husserl would describe reflective consciousness: thought turning towards itself.

Perhaps, then, wonder is not merely a reaction to something we see in the world, but a subtle manifestation of consciousness itself within us — the moment when thought observes that it is thinking, or simply that it is happening, or even that it is resting within itself.

pages.title: Spiele demokratischer Macht: Legalität, Moral und stiller Wille
pages.html:
KI-gestützte Übersetzung aus dem Griechischen. Griechisches Original

Demokratie, wie wir sie verstehen, ist nicht einfach der unmittelbare Ausdruck des gesellschaftlichen Willens, sondern ein komplexes System aus Verfahren, Regeln und gesetzgeberischen Konstruktionen. Wahlen, Quoten, Sitze und Beteiligungsregeln bilden zusammen ein Machtspiel, das die offizielle Legitimation häufig von der tatsächlichen gesellschaftlichen Zustimmung trennt. Die Frage der Wahlenthaltung, der leeren und ungültigen Stimmzettel sowie der Sitzverteilung kleiner Parteien offenbart nicht nur statistische oder zahlenmäßige Probleme, sondern auch eine tiefe moralische und existenzielle Ungleichheit.

In der Praxis werden bei griechischen Wahlen die Sitze auf der Grundlage gültiger Stimmen verteilt, während leere und ungültige Stimmzettel nur statistisch erfasst werden. Die Wahlenthaltung fließt nicht einmal in das offizielle Verhältnis der Sitze ein. Das bedeutet, dass ein Stimmenanteil einer Partei von 40 % der gültigen Stimmen bei einer Wahlbeteiligung von 50 % lediglich 20 % tatsächlicher gesellschaftlicher Unterstützung entspricht. Dasselbe gilt für alle anderen Parteien. Das Ergebnis ist, dass ein kleiner Prozentsatz der Bürger für die Mehrheit entscheiden kann, während die übrigen in den offiziellen Ergebnissen stumm oder unsichtbar bleiben.

Dieser Unterschied zwischen zahlenmäßiger Legalität und moralischer Autorität ist grundlegend. Obwohl das System den Willen der Minderheit in rechtmäßige Macht zu verwandeln scheint, spiegelt es nicht die tatsächliche gesellschaftliche Stärke wider. Die Wahlenthaltung, die bei den letzten Wahlen etwa 47 % der eingetragenen Wähler erreichte, und die leeren oder ungültigen Stimmzettel offenbaren einen stillen Protest, der jedoch politisch unsichtbar bleibt. Die Gesellschaft zeigt, dass ihre Vertretung weder die von ihr getroffene noch die nicht getroffene Wahl umfasst — Schweigen und die Verweigerung der Teilnahme sind also ebenso wichtig, werden aber institutionell nicht anerkannt.

Noch wichtiger ist, dass sich das System nicht darauf beschränkt, die stärkste Partei zu legitimieren. Es bringt auch andere Parteien mit geringen Sitzanteilen hervor — Parteien, die 1,5 %, 3 %, 6 % oder 10 % der eingetragenen Wähler erhalten. In der Praxis vertreten diese Parteien das Volk nicht substanziell, sondern fügen dem Spiel weitere Münder hinzu und erzeugen so die Illusion demokratischer Beteiligung. Dieser Zustand schafft ein tieferes moralisches Problem: Die Entscheidungen dieser kleinen Parteien scheinen dieselbe Autorität zu besitzen wie diejenigen der stärksten Partei, obwohl ihre gesellschaftliche Basis tatsächlich begrenzt ist. Die Gleichheit der Vertretung ist nur scheinbar — eine strukturierte Lüge, mit der das System Legitimität vortäuscht.

Die moralische Ungleichheit wird sichtbar, wenn wir fragen: Besitzt die Entscheidung einer Partei, die tatsächlich 20 % der Gesellschaft vertritt, dieselbe moralische Autorität wie die einer Partei, die 1,5 % vertritt? Dasselbe gilt für alle übrigen. Das Gesetzgebungsverfahren erscheint gerecht, legitimiert aber in Wirklichkeit Entscheidungen ohne gesellschaftliches Gewicht. Dadurch wird der demokratische Prozess zu einem Spiel, in dem Zahlen rechtmäßige Macht ohne tatsächliche gesellschaftliche Zustimmung erzeugen. Das ist der tiefere moralische Skandal, den du ansprichst: Gesetze und Regeln wurden nicht geschaffen, um dem Volk zu dienen, sondern um legitimierte Verfahren hervorzubringen, unabhängig davon, wer sie tatsächlich unterstützt.

Der stille Protest der Bürger, die sich enthalten oder leere beziehungsweise ungültige Stimmzettel abgeben, ist nicht bloße Untätigkeit. Er ist eine bewusste Entscheidung, das betrügerische Spiel nicht anzuerkennen. Die Bürger sehen, dass auch dann, wenn sie wählen, die Entscheidungen weiterhin von einer kleinen Minderheit getroffen werden und die übrigen Beteiligten keine wirkliche Vertretung beitragen, sondern nur scheinbare Legitimation. Die Wahlenthaltung wird hier zu einer politischen Ausdrucksform, die zeigt, dass die moralische Autorität der Macht nicht anerkannt wird.

Die Folge dieses Systems ist eine doppelte. Erstens verringert es das Vertrauen der Bürger in die Institutionen, weil sie verstehen, dass ihre Beteiligung im Wesentlichen nichts verändert. Zweitens verstärkt es die Konzentration von Macht bei kleinen Minderheiten, die zahlenmäßig, aber nicht moralisch legitimiert erscheinen. Mit diesem buchhalterischen Ansatz scheint Demokratie zu funktionieren, während sie im Kern die moralische Dimension gesellschaftlicher Zustimmung umgeht.

Besonders betrügerisch macht das Spiel die Legitimation durch falsche Gewichtungen: Das System stellt Entscheidungen kleiner Minderheiten als gleichwertig mit Entscheidungen dar, die eine breitere gesellschaftliche Basis hätten, während die tatsächlichen Zahlen und das Schweigen der Mehrheit unberücksichtigt bleiben. Die stärkste Partei mit 20 % tatsächlicher Unterstützung und die übrigen mit Anteilen von minimaler gesellschaftlicher Stärke entscheiden für alle anderen. So entsteht ein moralisches Defizit, das hinter der scheinbaren Stabilität des Systems unsichtbar bleibt.

Die moralische Dimension ist entscheidend. Es reicht nicht, darauf zu schauen, wer gewonnen hat, sondern darauf, wer das Recht hat, für die anderen zu entscheiden. Das System erkennt die gesellschaftliche Realität der Wahlenthaltung und der geringen Prozentanteile nicht an und verwandelt so eine Minderheit in Macht. Dadurch driften Legalität und moralische Autorität gefährlich auseinander. Wahlenthaltung, leere Stimmzettel und geringe Prozentanteile sind nicht bloß zahlenmäßige Phänomene, sondern zeigen, dass der Rahmen selbst infrage gestellt wird.

Demokratie, wie sie heute praktiziert wird, ist zugleich zahlenmäßig und existenziell: Die Rechnung scheint aufzugehen, die Gesellschaft sieht ein System, das „funktioniert“, doch die existenzielle und moralische Dimension offenbart, dass der tatsächliche Wille stumm oder ausgeschlossen bleibt. Die Spiele demokratischer Macht betreffen nicht nur die Frage, wer gewählt wird, sondern auch, wie die Gesellschaft ihrem Wesen nach vertreten wird und welche moralische Autorität die Macht besitzt, die aus rechtmäßigen, aber betrügerischen Verfahren hervorgeht.

Insgesamt ergibt sich folgendes Bild: Demokratie ist ein legitimiertes Verfahren, in dem kleine Minderheiten für alle entscheiden können, während die übrigen Beteiligten als „symbolische Vertreter“ ohne tatsächliche gesellschaftliche Stärke fungieren. Das Schweigen der Wahlenthaltung und die kalkulierte Beteiligung kleiner Parteien offenbaren das moralische Defizit und zeigen, dass der tatsächliche gesellschaftliche Wille nicht mit der offiziellen Legitimation übereinstimmt. Die Demokratie scheint zu funktionieren, spielt aber in Wirklichkeit ein betrügerisches Spiel, in dem die Arithmetik die Moral ersetzt und symbolische Stimmen Entscheidungen ohne tatsächliche gesellschaftliche Basis legitimieren.

pages.title: Jeux des pouvoirs démocratiques : légalité, morale et volonté silencieuse
pages.html:
Traduction du grec assistée par IA. Original grec

La démocratie telle que nous la concevons n’est pas simplement l’expression directe de la volonté sociale, mais un système complexe de procédures, de règles et de constructions législatives. Les élections, les quotas, les sièges, les règles de participation composent un jeu de pouvoir qui sépare souvent la légitimation officielle du véritable consentement social. La question de l’abstention, des bulletins blancs et nuls, ainsi que la répartition des sièges des petits partis, révèle non seulement des problèmes statistiques ou numériques, mais aussi une profonde inégalité morale et existentielle.

Sur le plan pratique, lors des élections grecques, les sièges sont répartis sur la base des suffrages valides, tandis que les bulletins blancs et nuls ne sont enregistrés qu’à des fins statistiques. L’abstention n’entre même pas dans le calcul officiel de la proportion des sièges. Cela signifie qu’un parti obtenant 40 % des suffrages valides dans un scrutin où la participation atteint 50 % ne dispose en réalité que de 20 % de soutien social. Il en va de même pour tous les autres partis. Il en résulte qu’un faible pourcentage de citoyens peut décider pour la majorité, tandis que les autres restent silencieux ou invisibles dans les résultats officiels.

Cette différence entre légalité numérique et autorité morale est fondamentale. Le système, tout en semblant transformer la volonté de la minorité en pouvoir légal, ne reflète pas la force sociale réelle.
